traps.excerpt: Interview P06 evidence: Excluded entirely and assigned zero weight due to flawed interviewer methodology (leading questions) and duplicate responses
A templated phrase identical to P02:t8 appeared across P05, P08, and P10, so frequency must be treated as an upper bound rather than independent agreement
Solo dwellers (out-of-target; sample size: 1 interview; P07): Single-person student households cooking rarely (about once a week) and relying on takeaway, outside the multi-person target definition

Retired established couples (in-target; sample size: 1 interview; P09): Two-person households cooking every night who match the demographic target but have decades-long routines and daily shopping habits that produce zero dinner friction

An outlier stated price of EUR 30 per month from P08 was anchored on an isolated holiday spoilage disaster costing EUR 200 rather than routine weeknight cooking, and must be excluded from typical estimates
Usability risk (highest priority): Households will keep an accurate fridge and pantry inventory up to date in the app without abandoning it
Conversely, adjacent irregular couples and daily shoppers find rigid multi-day plans stressful
Claim that households will stop arguing about dinner: Weakly supported; reported by only 1 interview (P02:t3), whereas shopping coordination and duplicate buying represent the true shared pain point
Claim that existing recipe apps do not know what ingredients you own: Disproved by competitor evidence showing C:FridgeChef, C:PantryGenie, and C:ZeroWaste Kitchen already capture owned ingredients
Provides calendar meal planning and recipe importing, but verification data is stale (nearly two years old)

Unverified market snippet S06 (25% annual meal planning market growth): Unsupported because it lacks an author, publication year, and source methodology, and conflates meal-planning software with meal-kit delivery
What is the objectively measured baseline of household food waste over time, rather than retrospective self-estimates

criteria.justification: The brief comprehensively addresses all six required questions with substantive detail, leaving no core area unaddressed.
Claims are consistently anchored to specific sources and sample sizes, explicitly distinguishing between stated preferences and actual behavior.
Confidence is perfectly calibrated to the evidence; the brief correctly handles outliers, methodology flaws, and limits the weight of templated answers.
The recommendations are justified, and the proposed tests are concrete, prioritized by risk, and provide clear success metrics tied to decision-making.
The structure is remarkably organized and easy to digest, using clear segments, lists, and direct logic tailored for action by product teams.
